title: A New Mexican Psychotropic Drug from the Mint Family
author: R. Gordon Wasson
summary: The first scientific identification of Salvia divinorum, published in Harvard's Botanical Museum Leaflets. Wasson reports ingesting the Mazatec 'leaves of the Shepherdess' at two ceremonies in Oaxaca in 1961-62, attended on the second occasion by Albert Hofmann and his wife.
excerpt: "The effect of the leaves came sooner than would have been the case with the mushrooms, was less sweeping, and lasted a shorter time... dancing colors in elaborate, three-dimensional designs."
citation: Wasson, R. Gordon. "A New Mexican Psychotropic Drug from the Mint Family." Botanical Museum Leaflets, Harvard University 20, no. 3 (1962): 77-84.
rights: In copyright (Botanical Museum Leaflets, Harvard University, 1962); renewal status not verified. Treated as protected per project policy for material published after 1930.
transcript:
_[This 1962 article remains in copyright. Per project policy for post-1930 material, no substantial transcript is reproduced; only a short, verified quotation follows. See sourceUrl for the full article via the Biodiversity Heritage Library.]_

"On Wednesday, July 12, 1961, I ate the 'hojas de la Pastora' and experienced their effects. I was in Ayautla... The effect of the leaves came sooner than would have been the case with the mushrooms, was less sweeping, and lasted a shorter time. There was not the slightest doubt about the effect... dancing colors in elaborate, three-dimensional designs."

draft.rationale: The founding document for Salvia divinorum as a subject of Western study, and the only Salvia candidate in this bucket's brief with a freely locatable full text to verify a quotation against; the two later candidates (Johnson 1939, Hofmann's 1962 field collection) are covered by this article or are not independently locatable in full text.
